summary: Root cause identified with medium confidence (0.72): portfolio-service deploy dep-5905 (v4.5.0, 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z) shipped a new unindexed query on the shared ledger-db, 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at', which executes as a Seq Scan over ~48.2M rows at 4-9s of CPU per call. This single statement accounts for essentially all of the ledger-db slow-query volume (1 -> ~139/min in the same minute), driving ledger-db CPU from ~30% to ~96% and connections from ~60 to ~185-200; order-service's INSERT INTO orders then queues behind the saturated CPU and is cancelled by the server-side statement timeout, producing the reported p99 > 5s. The 1-minute-resolution timeline confirms causation: ledger-db CPU/slow_queries/connections step simultaneously in the 08:58:00Z minute while order-service p99 stays ~148ms until 08:59:00Z, one minute later. The competing origins (autovacuum config change cfg-2903, untracked storage/IOPS event, order-service-local saturation) are each contradicted by timing, mechanism, or signature evidence.

ranked_hypotheses.title: portfolio-service deploy dep-5905: new unindexed query on trades (account_id + executed_at) drives ledger-db CPU/scan saturation
ranked_hypotheses.statement: portfolio-service v4.5.0 (dep-5905, 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z) added a new query 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at' on the shared ledger-db with no accompanying migration/index. Immediately after the deploy the query executes as a Seq Scan on trades over ~48M rows (F33), each execution consuming 4-9s of CPU (F34). Because ledger-db is shared (F11, F31) this drives ledger-db CPU from ~30% to ~96%, slow_queries_per_min from ~1 to ~140 and connections_active from ~60 to ~185-200, all stepping together in the 08:58Z minute (F21, F22, F23). order-service writes (INSERT INTO orders) then wait behind the CPU-bound DB work and are cancelled by the server-side statement timeout (F5, F19), which surfaces as order-service p99 stepping to seconds one minute later at 08:59Z (F24, F25, F26).

causal_chain.claim: portfolio-service v4.5.0 deployed at 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z adds a new ledger-db query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at, with 'no migration included' (dep-5905).
The new query runs as a sequential scan over the trades table (rows=48211907), i.e. no usable index on (account_id, executed_at).
Each execution of that query consumes multi-second CPU (4-9s per call, ~135-148 executions/min logged as slow), saturating ledger-db CPU.
ledger-db CPU, slow_queries_per_min and connections_active all step simultaneously in the 08:58:00Z minute, ~2 min after the 08:56 deploy, and stay pinned.
order-service latency stays flat through the 08:58 minute and rises one minute later at 08:59Z, consistent with being a downstream consequence of the DB step.
order-service INSERT INTO orders statements queue behind the CPU-bound work and are cancelled by the server-side statement timeout.
The cancelled/queued writes raise order-service p99 from ~150ms to the saturated ~5.2-5.4s steady state.

assumptions: The deploy's 08:56:00Z timestamp is the moment the new query code becomes live; the step appears in the 08:58 minute, a ~2-minute lag consistent with first request traffic reaching the new code path.
The single slow-query pattern observed IS the load driving the saturation; no other statement type became slow (F33, F37).
Execution frequency of the new query (~140/min) is a normal request rate for portfolio-service, i.e. it is not itself the anomaly — the sharing of an unindexed heavy query on a shared DB is.

ranked_hypotheses.title: DBA autovacuum change cfg-2903 (scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1 at 08:00Z) causes DB-wide I/O/CPU contention on ledger-db
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The DBA's more-aggressive autovacuum setting (cfg-2903, ledger-db, autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1, 2026-05-05T08:00Z) makes autovacuum run more often on ledger-db. Autovacuum workers consume CPU/IO, driving ledger-db CPU to ~95%, inflating connections and slow-query counts, so all clients — including order-service's INSERT INTO orders — stall and hit statement timeouts, producing the order-service p99 step.

causal_chain.claim: DBA changes ledger-db autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1 at 2026-05-05T08:00Z (cfg-2903), the only ledger-db config change in the window.
More aggressive autovacuum triggers frequent/large vacuum runs on ledger-db.
Vacuum work saturates ledger-db CPU and I/O, raising slow_queries_per_min and active connections in the 08:49-08:58 step.
Order-service writes queue behind the contention and are cancelled by statement timeout, raising p99.

assumptions: The scale_factor change actually produced a vacuum burst — no vacuum-activity metric or DBA/PostgreSQL log was queried, so the effect is unobserved.
A 0.2 -> 0.1 scale_factor change could move a steady-state DB from 30% to 95% CPU; this is a modest tuning delta and the effect claim is not evidenced.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Three verified facts rule it out. (1) Timing: the change was applied at 08:00Z, but no metric moves for ~58 minutes; ledger-db is flat through 08:57 and steps only in the 08:58:00Z minute (F21, F22, F23) — a vacuum burst would begin promptly, not after a near-hour delay. (2) Mechanism: autovacuum activity in the window touched only public.audit_log (9 times, 08:08:06-09:59:49) and never the trades or orders tables (F37); there is no vacuum contention on the relevant tables. (3) Scope/symptom mismatch: the entire slow-query volume is a single portfolio-service SELECT seq-scanning trades (F33), not vacuum-driven I/O; and zero lock/block/vacuum-wait events were logged (F36), while the pre-onset baseline had no vacuum contention at all (F38). The reporter's suspicion is thus contradicted by the data.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Untracked ledger-db infra/storage event (IOPS throttling / burst-credit exhaustion) degrades the shared DB
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An infra-level event on ledger-db's storage — e.g. cloud volume burst credits exhausted, causing IOPS throttling as in HIST-110 (F13) — begins around 08:58Z, making all DB I/O slow. CPU rises as queries wait on I/O, slow_queries and connections climb, and every client including order-service's INSERT INTO orders times out. No application change is required; the tracked deploy and config change merely coincide.

causal_chain.claim: A storage/IOPS-level event begins on ledger-db's volume around 08:58Z (untracked; HIST-110 precedent).
DB queries become I/O-bound: CPU pinned ~95%, slow_queries ~140/min, connections tripled.
Order-service writes stall and are cancelled by statement timeout, raising order-service p99.

assumptions: No IOPS/disk-latency/burst-credit metric is exposed for ledger-db, so this cannot be confirmed or refuted with available data.
The step coincides with a tracked deploy (F7) and a tracked config change (F8), which is a coincidence under this hypothesis.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: The mechanism is now contradicted rather than merely untested. F33/F34 show the slow-query load is a single identifiable portfolio-service SELECT doing 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)' at 4-9s CPU per execution — that is CPU-bound scan work, not I/O-wait from throttled storage. F18 shows disk_used_pct and replication_lag_ms flat and uncorrelated with onset, and F33/F34 identify an application query as the load source, so a pure storage-burst event is not needed and is inconsistent with the observed single-statement pattern. Retained as rejected but explicit: no IOPS metric exists to fully falsify it.

ranked_hypotheses.title: order-service-local saturation (pool exhaustion / retry storm) presenting as DB statement timeouts
ranked_hypotheses.statement: order-service itself saturates — connection/thread pool exhaustion or a retry storm — so its requests queue locally and its writes exceed the DB statement timeout while queued, appearing as ledger-db statement timeouts without the DB being the primary fault.

causal_chain.claim: order-service local pool/thread saturation or retry storm occurs (no deploy or config change to order-service; F9, F10).
Queued writes exceed the statement timeout and are cancelled, and p99 rises.

assumptions: Would require order-service-local resource pressure that no observed metric shows.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F20 shows order-service CPU flat at ~39-41% with db_pool_in_use rising from ~14 to ~46 — connections queuing on a slow DB, not local saturation. ledger-db CPU/slow_queries/connections saturate one minute earlier (F21, F22, F23). F9/F10 show no order-service deploy or config change to trigger local exhaustion, and errors are server-side statement timeouts (F19), not pool-acquisition failures.

facts.statement: Exactly one deployment occurred across all services on 2026-05-05: portfolio-service v4.5.0 (dep-5905) at 08:56:00Z by k.shah, described as adding a 'new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at' with 'no migration included', status 'live' (not rolled back).
No order-service deployment exists in any observed window, and no deployments or config changes were recorded on 2026-05-03 or 2026-05-04.
Exactly one config change occurred in the window: cfg-2903 on ledger-db, autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1 at 2026-05-05T08:00:00Z by dba-team.

All 185 ledger-db slow-query WARN entries between 08:45Z and 10:00Z are one identical statement: portfolio-service's 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at', executing as 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)', first seen 08:58:38Z; it is the only slow-query pattern present.

Per-execution latency of the portfolio-service trades query is 4-9s per call (repeatedly 8690ms, 8257ms, 8823ms, 8728ms, 4189-8749ms through 09:11:37), i.e. the query directly consumes multi-second CPU per execution.

At 1-minute resolution, ledger-db cpu_pct is flat through the 08:56 (28.92) and 08:57 (32.14) buckets and first rises in the 08:58:00Z bucket (95.62%), pinned 94-97% thereafter; no minute strictly before 08:56:00Z shows any rise.
ledger-db slow_queries_per_min is flat through 08:57 (08:55=1.07, 08:56=1.52, 08:57=1.33) and jumps to 139.17 in the 08:58:00Z minute, simultaneous with the cpu_pct jump.
ledger-db connections_active is flat ~60-65 through 08:57 and jumps to 185.11 in the 08:58:00Z minute; all three ledger-db signals step in the SAME 08:58:00Z minute.
order-service latency_p99_ms stays flat ~143-167ms through the 08:56, 08:57 and 08:58 buckets and only jumps in the 08:59:00Z minute to 5607.8ms, one minute AFTER the ledger-db signals step at 08:58.

order-service's only ERROR pattern is a server-side statement timeout on writes: 'ledger-db: canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)', 284 occurrences, first_seen 2026-05-05T09:00:42Z through 10:58:29Z.
order-service shows no local resource saturation: CPU stayed flat ~39-41% across the whole window while db_pool_in_use rose from ~14 to ~45-46 from 09:02 onward.

order-service's 'INSERT INTO orders' does NOT appear as a slow query on ledger-db (total_matched=0 for 08:45-10:00Z); autovacuum activity touched only public.audit_log (9 times, 08:08:06-09:59:49) and never the trades or orders tables.
ZERO blocking/lock/wait evidence exists on ledger-db in 08:45-10:00Z: log queries for 'lock', 'block' and 'wait' each returned total_matched=0.
The pre-onset ledger-db baseline (06:00-08:45Z) contains only ONE WARN entry, an unrelated clock-drift/NTP message at 06:44:41Z; no slow queries, locks or vacuum contention existed before the step.
ledger-db disk_used_pct stayed flat at ~70.9-71.3% and replication_lag_ms flat at ~39-41ms across the entire 06:00-10:59 window, including through onset.

ledger-db is a shared postgres owned by platform, shared=true, with direct db callers order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service, confirming portfolio-service's new trades query runs against the same instance that serves order-service.
order-service p99 latency was flat ~146-154ms avg from 06:00 to 08:48, then stepped abruptly to ~5200-5400ms steady state from 09:02 onward; the reported 'p99 > 5s' is that saturated steady state.
No pgbouncer/proxy or pool-configuration node is exposed for ledger-db: its dependency view returns the node with no proxy/pooler edge between callers and the postgres.

assumptions: The deploy timestamp 08:56:00Z is the moment the new query code becomes live; the load step appears in the 08:58:00Z minute, a ~2-minute lag consistent with first production traffic reaching the new code path.
The portfolio-service trades query runs at roughly its normal request rate (~140/min); the anomaly is the sharing of an unindexed heavy query on a shared DB, not the raw request volume.
The single slow-query pattern observed is the load driving the saturation; no other statement type became slow.

The observed Seq Scan over 48.2M rows at 4-9s per call is taken as proof the query is not using an efficient index path, even though the (account_id, executed_at) index inventory itself could not be checked.
order-service statement timeouts are a downstream consequence of ledger-db CPU saturation, not an independent order-service fault (supported by order-service CPU flat and no order-service change).

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Direction of dependency at onset: ledger-db degradation (08:58) leads order-service latency degradation (08:59) by one minute, while order-service p99 is flat through 08:58 with the DB already at 95% CPU.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) The deploy metadata states the new query shipped with 'no migration included', i.e. no schema/index migration accompanied it; this is a plan statement, not confirmation that no (account_id, executed_at) index exists.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Historical precedent HIST-111 (2025-05-22): 'Reporting job full table scans slowed ledger-db', root cause 'new report query without index did sequential scans', category bad_deployment, resolution 'Added index; query review gate'.

timeline.event: Config change cfg-2903 applied on ledger-db: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1 by dba-team ('More aggressive autovacuum'). No metric change follows for ~58 minutes.
portfolio-service v4.5.0 deployed (dep-5905) by k.shah; adds the new trades query (account_id + executed_at) with no migration included; status live.
All three ledger-db signals step simultaneously in this minute: cpu_pct 32.14 -> 95.62%, slow_queries_per_min 1.33 -> 139.17, connections_active ~60 -> 185.11.
First ledger-db slow-query WARN: portfolio-service's 'SELECT * FROM trades ... ORDER BY executed_at' logged as 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)' at 8690ms.
order-service latency_p99_ms jumps from ~148.62ms (08:58) to 5607.8ms, one minute after the ledger-db step.
First order-service ERROR: 'ledger-db: canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)'; 284 occurrences through 10:58:29Z.
order-service p99 reaches the saturated steady state (~5200-5400ms), which is the reported 'p99 > 5s'; db_pool_in_use ~45-46 while order-service CPU stays flat ~40%.
Incident INC-009 reported by on-call SRE.
Latest data: ledger-db CPU pinned ~95-97%, slow_queries ~142/min, connections ~182-197; deploy dep-5905 still live (not rolled back).

recommended_actions.action: Immediate mitigation: disable/revert the code path introduced by dep-5905 (portfolio-service v4.5.0) that issues the new trades query, or roll back portfolio-service to the pre-4.5.0 version. This is the named change driving the load.
recommended_actions.rationale: F7/F28 identify dep-5905 as the sole deployment in the window and the change that added the query; F33/F34 show that query is the single statement generating ~140 slow queries/min and the 4-9s CPU per call. Removing the load should return ledger-db to its ~30% baseline and clear order-service's statement timeouts (F21, F22, F23).

recommended_actions.action: Verify mitigation: after disabling/rolling back, confirm ledger-db cpu_pct returns toward ~30%, slow_queries_per_min to ~1/min, and connections_active to ~60, and that order-service p99 returns to ~146-154ms with no new 'canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)' errors.
recommended_actions.rationale: These are the exact signals that stepped at 08:58 and 08:59 (F21, F22, F23, F24, F5, F19); their return to baseline confirms the mechanism and clears the incident.

recommended_actions.action: Fix the query: add an index on ledger-db trades (account_id, executed_at) (or otherwise fix the access path for the new query), then re-enable the portfolio-service feature only after confirming the plan is an index scan rather than 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)'.
recommended_actions.rationale: F33 shows the query executes as a Seq Scan over ~48.2M rows and F29 records the deploy shipped with 'no migration included'; the exact remediation matches HIST-111 (F32, F13).

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT revert cfg-2903 (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1) as an incident mitigation, and do not treat the autovacuum change as causal.
recommended_actions.rationale: H2 is rejected: the 08:00Z change precedes onset by ~58 minutes with no metric movement, autovacuum touched only public.audit_log and never trades/orders (F37), and there are zero lock/block/vacuum-wait events (F36) with a clean pre-onset baseline (F38). Reverting it would not address the observed single-statement CPU-bound load.

recommended_actions.action: Prevent recurrence: add a pre-deploy query-review gate that requires EXPLAIN/plan verification and a supporting index migration for any new query against shared ledger-db, with a load test against production-scale data before rollout.
recommended_actions.rationale: The identical failure mode occurred in HIST-111 (unindexed new report query causing full table scans on ledger-db), whose recorded resolution was 'Added index; query review gate' (F32, F13). A shared, multi-caller DB (F11, F31) makes one caller's unindexed query a cross-service availability risk.

recommended_actions.action: Improve detection/telemetry on ledger-db: expose per-statement latency/rows-examined and an index/plan inventory (or at least a statement-level slow-query counter), and alert on slow_queries_per_min and connections_active so a step like 1 -> 139/min is caught before downstream statement timeouts.
recommended_actions.rationale: The investigation could not confirm index existence or the access path at the source, and had no per-statement metrics — only log text (data gaps). Detecting the 08:58 step directly would have surfaced the cause minutes earlier than the 09:00:42 downstream timeouts (F5).

data_gaps: Index existence on ledger-db trades (account_id, executed_at) could NOT be confirmed at the source: no schema/index-listing, EXPLAIN, or rows-examined telemetry exists. The core mechanism is inferred from the observed Seq Scan plus the deploy's 'no migration included' metadata (F29, F33).

No IOPS/disk-latency/burst-credit metric is exposed for ledger-db (available metrics are cpu_pct, connections_active, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min), so H3 (untracked storage/IOPS event) cannot be fully falsified — it is rejected on mechanism (single CPU-bound seq scan, F33/F34) and flat disk/replication signals (F18), not by direct IOPS measurement.

No ledger-db PostgreSQL/DBA server logs were queried, so the autovacuum change's actual runtime effect is unobserved (H2 rejected on timing, vacuum-table scope F37, and absence of lock/block/wait events F36).
No pgbouncer/proxy or pool-configuration node is exposed for ledger-db (dependency edges empty, F30), so a pool-side explanation for the connection/CPU step can be neither included nor excluded.

Blast radius was not enumerated: budget exhaustion prevented querying other ledger-db callers (payment-service, settlement-service) or their per-service onset times, so it is not proven from direct observation that this is ledger-db-wide rather than order-service-specific (though ledger-db CPU/slow-query/connection saturation implicates the shared DB).
The order-service ERROR log result was truncated (25 of 284 matches), so additional error patterns beyond the INSERT-timeout signature cannot be excluded.

portfolio-service's own latency/logs and any portfolio-service config/flag changes were not queried, so the exact moment its query starts executing at 08:58 is inferred from the ledger-db slow-query log at 08:58:38Z rather than observed directly at the caller.

order-service deploy history for the preceding week was not fully executed in one query path, so 'order-service has not been released this week' is corroborated only by the all-services windows checked (F9, F10).
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that ledger-db's CPU/slow-query saturation had a onset strictly before 08:56:00Z at 1-minute resolution (e.g. a sustained rise in a pre-08:56 minute) would break the temporal link to dep-5905 and re-open H2/H3.

Discovery that an index on trades (account_id, executed_at) already exists, and that the logged Seq Scan is caused by something other than a missing index (e.g. stale statistics or a forced plan), would change the specific fix but not the identification of the new query as the load source.
Evidence that the 185 slow-query entries are generated by a client other than portfolio-service (mislabeled or second client with an identical statement) would redirect the origin.
A real autovacuum burst on trades/orders evidenced by vacuum logs or a vacuum-wait/IO signal correlated with 08:58 would revive H2; currently contradicted by F36, F37, F38.

An IOPS/disk-latency metric showing throttling onset at 08:58 would support H3; currently contradicted by the single CPU-bound seq-scan signature (F33, F34) and flat disk_used_pct/replication_lag (F18).

Evidence of order-service-local resource saturation (CPU/memory/restart or pool-acquisition errors) at onset would revive H4; currently contradicted by F19 (server-side statement timeout) and F20 (flat CPU, pool queuing).

ledger-db CPU steps in the same 08:55 bucket as order-service latency: from a stable ~29-30% baseline (06:00-08:48) to 67.67% avg (max 96.36) at 08:55, then pinned at ~95-97% from 09:02 onward.
ledger-db slow_queries_per_min steps in the same 08:55 bucket: from ~0.8-1.2/min baseline (06:00-08:48) to 82.59 avg (max 148.81) at 08:55, then sustained ~135-143/min.

ledger-db connections_active steps in the same 08:55 bucket: from ~60-64 baseline to 134.52 avg (max 199.81) at 08:55, then ~186-199, while disk_used_pct stays flat ~71% throughout (not a disk-space issue).

Sequence at 1-minute resolution: ledger-db CPU/slow_queries/connections first rise in the 08:58:00Z minute; order-service p99 first rises in the 08:59:00Z minute. The first sustained rise of BOTH is strictly AT or AFTER 08:56:00Z — no sustained rise begins strictly BEFORE 08:56:00Z. The finer resolution places onset ~2–3 min later than the 7-min bucket implied (08:49/08:55 buckets straddled 08:56 because coarse buckets blended flat 08:55–08:57 minutes with the 08:58 jump).

Direction of dependency at onset: ledger-db degradation (08:58) leads order-service latency degradation (08:59) by one minute, and order-service p99 is flat through 08:58 while the DB is already at 95% CPU — consistent with order-service latency being a downstream consequence of the ledger-db step rather than an independent order-service fault.

findings.statement: The deploy's own metadata states the new query was shipped with 'no migration included' — i.e. no schema/index migration accompanied it. This is the closest deploy metadata to an index fact, but it is a plan statement, NOT a confirmation that no (account_id, executed_at) index exists on ledger-db's trades table; no index-inventory, EXPLAIN, or rows-examined telemetry for the trades table is available in any tool queried.

No pgbouncer/proxy or pool-configuration data for ledger-db is exposed: its dependency view returns the node with edges:[] (no proxy/pooler node between callers and the postgres), and the historical search for a pgbouncer/pool-exhaustion precedent returned only incidents about order-service's OWN datasource pool (HIST-115) and a ledger-db primary failover (HIST-102) — none about a ledger-db-side proxy or its pool config.

ledger-db's direct caller set (upstream, caller->callee) is exactly order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service, each via kind 'db'; ledger-db is a shared postgres owned by platform. This confirms portfolio-service's new trades query runs against the same shared instance that serves order-service.

The most on-point precedent for H1's mechanism is HIST-111 (2025-05-22, ledger-db/settlement-service): 'Reporting job full table scans slowed ledger-db', root_cause 'New report query without index did sequential scans', category bad_deployment, resolution 'Added index; query review gate' — a lead consistent with a new-query-without-index seq scan, but explicitly a past incident and not evidence about the current one.
